about: Hand-written story records. Load with scripts/load_story_seed.py. `hash` is scenario_catalog.text_hash of the question; the order of items inside a chapter's stage is the play order.

items.beat: Ines opens with the oldest wish on the backlog: tests for the billing module nobody dares to touch.
items.win: The agent maps the module first, and each finding shapes the next task. Coverage grows where it matters.
items.fail: The fixed plan meets code nobody predicted, and half the subtasks turn out to be pointless.

items.beat: A deprecated logging library has to go, and two engineers already disagree on how.
items.win: The approach is settled before the first edit, and sixty files change the same way.
items.fail: Thirty files in, the approach proves wrong and the work starts over.

items.beat: Reconciliation corrupts data now and then, and the team lead wants no file touched before the fix is reviewed.
items.win: Claude investigates freely, the lead reviews the approach, and only then does code change.
items.fail: The lead finds edits in the diff before anything was reviewed, and the session is thrown away.

items.beat: The new legacy-explorer subagent is configured and ready. Claude acts as if it did not exist.
items.win: Exploration now goes to legacy-explorer, and the main conversation stays light.
items.fail: The main agent keeps reading every file itself and runs out of room.

items.beat: The team dashboard chokes on the module records the analyzer sends it.
items.win: Every record now arrives in the agreed shape, and the dashboard stops dropping modules.
items.fail: Malformed records keep slipping through, and the dashboard still shows gaps.

items.beat: Controllers come out perfect. Then someone asks for a background worker and gets route handlers.
items.win: Workers look like workers and migrations like migrations.
items.fail: The next migration script still arrives with controller annotations.

items.beat: The browser checks work on one engineer's laptop. Everyone else who clones the repository gets nothing.
items.win: A fresh clone now brings the server along, with one approval per developer.
items.fail: New clones still come without the server, and the page of manual setup steps grows.

items.beat: The docs-search server should come with the repository, but it needs a token and security is watching.
items.win: The configuration is in the repository, the token is not, and security signs off.
items.fail: Security blocks the merge, or the server only works for whoever set it up.

items.beat: Claude's boilerplate commits land on pull requests, yet every one of those pull requests is stuck.
items.win: Checks run on Claude's commits, and the pull requests can merge again.
items.fail: The commits keep arriving without checks, and the pull requests stay blocked.

items.beat: A migration reached the database without its dry run, and it was a destructive one.
items.win: No migration can be applied now without a passed dry run, whatever the agent decides.
items.fail: A few weeks later another migration skips its dry run.

items.beat: The docs-writer subagent documents private helpers the main agent had already ruled out.
items.win: The documentation covers the public API only, and nothing is explored twice.
items.fail: The subagent explores from scratch again and documents the helpers again.

items.beat: The service catalog lists owning teams that never existed.
items.win: Where a file says nothing, the catalog now says nothing.
items.fail: The catalog still passes validation and still contains invented teams.

items.beat: Engineers cannot check the onboarding document's claims, and a disagreement between two subagents vanished from it.
items.win: Every claim points to a file, and where subagents disagree the document shows both.
items.fail: New engineers still cannot verify the document and stop trusting it.

items.beat: Since the browser server and its 25 tools were added, the main agent fumbles its everyday tools.
items.win: The browser tools load only where they are used, and the main agent is sharp again.
items.fail: The main agent still carries 25 tool descriptions it never uses.

items.beat: Two hours into the billing exploration, the agent starts talking about billing systems in general.
items.win: The findings outlive the conversation, and hour three is as precise as minute ten.
items.fail: By the afternoon the agent contradicts what it found in the morning.

items.beat: Yesterday's dependency trace is a day old, and six of its files moved overnight.
items.win: The agent keeps what still holds and checks again what moved. The report is right.
items.fail: The report lists files that no longer exist.

items.beat: The support agent became a coordinator with specialists, but billing disputes never reach the billing specialist.
items.win: Billing disputes now go to the specialist that knows the rules.
items.fail: The coordinator keeps handling disputes itself, and keeps getting proration wrong.

items.beat: A customer writes again two days later, and the request lands on a container that has never seen the case.
items.win: Any container picks up the conversation where it stopped.
items.fail: The agent greets the customer as a stranger and asks everything again.

items.beat: Traces show lookup_order called with email addresses, and called for questions it cannot answer.
items.win: The agent now sends order IDs, and only when an order is the question.
items.fail: The validation errors and the wasted turns continue.

items.beat: Refund policies sit in nested folders of markdown, and a dispute turns on every mention of a restocking fee.
items.win: The agent finds exactly the documents that mention the fee and loads only those.
items.fail: The agent loads far too much, or misses a regional policy.

items.beat: A new hook cleans up refund amounts. Since it went live, every refund call it touches fails.
items.win: Refund calls go through again, with numeric amounts.
items.fail: Intercepted refunds still fail validation.

items.beat: The agent escalates easy corrections from angry customers and keeps the truly unclear disputes. First-contact resolution sits at 64%.
items.win: Escalations now follow the case, not the tone, and the resolution rate climbs.
items.fail: Strong language still triggers escalation, and the rate stays at 64%.

items.beat: Claude Code follows the wrapper conventions for the team lead and ignores them for the two newest engineers.
items.win: Everyone who clones the repository gets the conventions.
items.fail: The next new engineer gets a Claude Code that has never heard of the conventions.

items.beat: The triage checklist changed, but one developer's /triage-refund still runs the old steps.
items.win: That developer now gets the team's checklist like everyone else.
items.fail: The old steps keep running on that one machine.

items.beat: Omar wants every pull request on the refund tools reviewed by Claude in CI, with a script deciding pass or fail.
items.win: The pipeline reads the review and fails the build on critical findings, with nobody involved.
items.fail: The job waits for input nobody will give, or produces text the script cannot read.

items.beat: Human agents receive one-line escalation notes and start every case from zero.
items.win: Every ticket now arrives complete, and handling time drops by half.
items.fail: Notes get longer on some days and stay one line on others.

items.beat: A summary said a refund had been issued. Only the customer had said so; the order lookup showed none.
items.win: Reviewers see where each fact came from, and where customer and system disagree.
items.fail: Reviewers still cannot tell fact from claim, and check everything again.

items.beat: Auditors find policy-breaking refunds in 6% of cases, and the agent had double-checked every one of them.
items.win: Flawed refunds are now stopped before the money moves.
items.fail: The agent keeps agreeing with itself, and the auditors keep finding the same cases.

items.beat: Shipping, loyalty and subscriptions arrive: 18 tools instead of 4, and the agent starts picking the wrong ones.
items.win: Each kind of request meets a small set of tools, and the right one gets picked.
items.fail: Loyalty tools still fire in the middle of billing disputes.

items.beat: Forty-five turns into a dispute, the agent quotes the wrong amount and asks for a decision the customer already made.
items.win: The amount, the orders and the customer's choice stay exact however long the conversation runs.
items.fail: After the next summary the agreed amount is gone again.

items.beat: QA wants all 5,000 conversations of the day reviewed overnight, and leadership wants the bill smaller.
items.win: The audit runs overnight at a lower price, and live customers wait no longer than before.
items.fail: Either the bill stays high, or customers start waiting for answers.

items.beat: The test-gap subagent hands back textbook advice that never mentions the pull request it was given.
items.win: Its findings now name the changed modules and the failures already collected.
items.fail: The advice stays generic, and developers skip it.

items.beat: Two headless steps in one job: the second must build on everything the first found, and other jobs share the runner.
items.win: The second step continues the first one's work, whatever else runs beside it.
items.fail: A step picks up another job's context, and tests appear for the wrong pull request.

items.beat: Developers have stopped reading the reviewer's comments, the real bugs included.
items.win: There are fewer comments, and the ones that remain are worth reading.
items.fail: Naming remarks keep coming, and the next real bug goes unread.

items.beat: Review comments come out in a different structure on every run, and the posting step keeps failing to parse them.
items.win: Comments arrive in one structure, and the posting step stops failing.
items.fail: The structure still drifts from run to run.

items.beat: Generated tests often do not compile, and engineers repair them by hand before merging.
items.win: Tests arrive already passing against the current code.
items.fail: Engineers still fix generated tests before every merge.

items.beat: Claude's edit to the shared lint configuration fails: the text it wants to replace appears in several places.
items.win: Only the intended block changes.
items.fail: The edit fails again, or the wrong block changes.

items.beat: Reviews can read ticket context on one engineer's machine, and nowhere else.
items.win: Every clone and every runner now has the ticket server, and no credential is in the repository.
items.fail: CI reviews still run without ticket context.

items.beat: Migration files need strict security review conventions, but most review runs never touch a migration.
items.win: The conventions load when a migration is in the diff and stay out of the way otherwise.
items.fail: Either every run pays for the conventions, or migrations get reviewed without them.

items.beat: With --bare, CI runs start clean every time. They also stopped using the security reviewer subagent.
items.win: The subagent is back in CI, and startup is still the same on every runner.
items.fail: The main agent keeps doing the whole analysis alone and fills its context.

items.beat: When GitHub times out, the whole review run is abandoned instead of the one comment being tried again.
items.win: A timeout now costs one retry instead of a whole review.
items.fail: The next GitHub hiccup kills another review run.

items.beat: On large pull requests the findings JSON arrives cut off in the middle of an array.
items.win: Cut-off replies are noticed and asked for again with enough room.
items.fail: The loop retries, and the JSON is cut off at the same place.

items.beat: After the nightly batch, some generated tests were committed against the wrong source files.
items.win: Every result finds its own file, whatever order the results come in.
items.fail: A reordered results file mixes up the tests again.

items.beat: On pull requests with 40 files the reviewer contradicts itself and misses changes that span files.
items.win: Each file gets full attention, and what spans files is caught as well.
items.fail: The reviewer still flags a pattern in one file and approves it in the next.

items.beat: Past the hundredth file, review comments turn vague and start to contradict the early ones.
items.win: The last file gets the same grounded review as the first.
items.fail: Late files still get comments about typical patterns.

items.beat: Most disputed comments concern patterns the guidelines say nothing about, posted as if they were settled.
items.win: Judgment calls go to a person, and clear findings get posted.
items.fail: Developers keep contesting findings the guidelines never covered.

items.beat: The prototype loop waits for the words RESEARCH COMPLETE. Some runs stop early, others never stop.
items.win: Runs end when the work is done, whatever words the model chooses.
items.fail: A finding that happens to contain the phrase ends another run early.

items.beat: A turn limit of 5 keeps costs down and ends every complex research topic before its report.
items.win: Complex topics finish, and spending still has a ceiling.
items.fail: Runs either stop early again or cost without limit.

items.beat: The analysis subagent searches cached web pages for material that only exists in the internal archive, and the reverse.
items.win: Each search goes to the corpus that holds the material.
items.fail: Half the lookups still go to the wrong corpus.

items.beat: Findings arrive with inline citations, footnotes or no date at all, and the synthesis agent misattributes claims.
items.win: Findings arrive in one format, the undated ones included.
items.fail: The format keeps varying, and claims keep getting the wrong source.

items.beat: Three tools report time in three formats, and the synthesis agent puts events in the wrong order.
items.win: Every timestamp reaches the agents in one format, and the chronology holds.
items.fail: Now and then a date is still misread, and the timeline is wrong again.

items.beat: Test files sit next to the code in every package, and the testing conventions should load only when one is touched.
items.win: The conventions appear with test files and cost nothing otherwise.
items.fail: The conventions either load in every session or are missed in some packages.

items.beat: Prompt templates are scattered across four packages and need strict citation formatting whenever someone edits one.
items.win: Anyone editing a template gets the conventions, straight from the repository.
items.fail: The conventions reach some folders and some teammates only.

items.beat: Claude published an unfinished draft to the whole distribution channel, on its own.
items.win: The command is still in the menu, and only a person can run it.
items.fail: Another draft goes out, or the skill disappears from the menu.

items.beat: In 9% of runs the report is written before synthesis has finished, and citations are missing.
items.win: The report writer cannot start until synthesis has delivered.
items.fail: The ordering still slips now and then, and reports go out incomplete.

items.beat: Every failed document fetch looks the same to the subagent, which retries a few times and then drops the source.
items.win: The subagent fixes a bad ID, waits out a rate limit and reports what is restricted.
items.fail: Sources keep disappearing from the analysis without a reason given.

items.beat: Sources without a publication date end up with one anyway, and the timeline logic breaks.
items.win: Undated sources stay undated, and the timeline can be trusted.
items.fail: Invented dates keep entering the reports.

items.beat: Search timeouts leave whole topic areas out of the final report, and nobody is told.
items.win: The coordinator knows what failed and what was found, and works around it.
items.fail: The coordinator repeats the same query, and the report still has silent gaps.

items.beat: Thirty-page reports go to one reviewer agent, which checks the opening carefully and the rest less so.
items.win: Page 28 gets the same scrutiny as page 2, and the statistics agree throughout.
items.fail: Citation errors in the later sections still get through.

items.beat: Leadership wants less human review. Overall citation accuracy is 96%, and niche science reports are a small share.
items.win: Reviewers see the doubtful claims, and spot checks keep the rest honest.
items.fail: Review is cut on the strength of one number, and the weak segment goes unseen.
